newsitem.title: SWAZILAND: Swazi government deploys troops as workers strike.
newsitem.headline: Swazi government deploys troops as workers strike.

text.p: Heavily armed soldiers and police were deployed across Swaziland on Monday, dampening a national strike called by unions to demand greater democracy in the tiny landlocked kingdom.
Security forces set up roadblocks and policemen stood guard over banks, shops and businesses that were closed for the day.
Most factories in the sugar belt region were reported shut and the public sector was said to be 50 percent operational. Schools and Swaziland's only university were also closed.

Police reported no incidents of violence. The industrial centre Manzini was tense, however, after police fired warning shots into the air to break up a skirmish at a bus rank after a petrol bomb was lit. No one was arrested and no one was hurt.
Western diplomats said the force used by the government to quell the strike amounted to a virtual state of emergency.

"The only thing they don't have is a curfew but the government has done a very efficient job and the measures are so comprehensive that we have a de facto state of emergency," one diplomat told Reuters.
Prime Minister Sibusiso Dlamini denounced the strike as unjustified and damaging to the kingdom's economy in an open letter in the daily Swazi Observer newspaper on Monday.
"A mass stayaway would deliver a body blow to Swaziland's economy...There would also be a very serious negative effect on the potential investments that Swaziland desperately needs."

In a plea to give the Swazi government time to introduce democratic changes, he added: "Government is aware that a reassessment of the political structure is needed and is acting to facilitate this," he added.

Political observers said the weekend arrest of four Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions' leaders on charges of contravening the Public Order Act and disagreement between some unions over the timing of the strike had blunted the stayaway call.
"There is less public sympathy for SFTU and also they have come to hear of wrangling in the SFTU about the merits of the strike," said one observer, who declined to be named.
South Africa's largest trade union federation, COSATU, has called on the Swazi government to release the four union leaders or face a go-slow in the handling of goods from Swaziland.
Swaziland is heavily dependent on neighbouring South Africa, which absorbs more than half of the country's exports.
The SFTU was part of a democratic alliance formed late last year to force the repeal of a 1973 decree which vested all the state's powers in the monarch.
After a violent strike in early 1996, reigning King Mswati III set up a review commission with a mandate to review the constitution and make recommendations for democratic change.
South Africa's foreign affairs department issued a carefully worded statement on Monday, saying Pretoria regretted the union leaders' arrest and backed moves towards democracy in Swaziland.
"In a fraternal spirit, South Africa wishes to encourage the government of Swaziland to enter into dialogue with all sectors of Swaziland society," it added.
South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo is to meet his Swazi counterpart Arthur Khoza in Pretoria on Tuesday to discuss the strike and calls for quicker political transformation.
